# The Unfinished Map

I keep a map of a city that does not exist. It is drawn in pencil on a piece of drafting paper that has yellowed at the edges. The streets have names like Ashwind Passage and Hourglass Row. There is a river that loops in an impossible knot through the old quarter, and a tram line that stops at a station drawn as a tiny circle with no name. The map is not finished. It will never be finished. I add a street now and then, erase a bridge, smudge a coastline. I have been working on it for eleven years. It is the most honest thing I own.

We are taught early that unfinished things are failures. A half-read book, a half-written letter, a half-built model airplane gather dust and guilt in equal measure. Completion is a moral virtue. Resolve is a muscle. Finish what you start. But I have come to believe that unfinished things are not the opposite of finished things. They are a different order of being. They are alive in a way that finished things are not. A finished map is a record. An unfinished map is a conversation.

The city on my map changes because I change. When I was twenty-two, I drew a grand boulevard leading to a capitol building with a dome. I was certain about that dome. It represented something—ambition, maybe, or the idea that a person should have a center. A decade later, I erased the capitol and let the boulevard dwindle into a farmer's market that only opens on Tuesdays. The map did not mourn. It accepted the alteration the way a river accepts a new channel.

There are places on the map I have never drawn because I do not yet know what they are. They appear as blank spaces, which is not the same as emptiness. If you look at a real map, the blank spaces are often the most interesting parts. Terra incognita, the old cartographers wrote. Unknown land. But they did not leave those spaces blank out of ignorance. They left them blank out of respect. A map with no blank spaces is a lie. It pretends that the world has no mystery. My city has a large blank space in the northwest quadrant. I have walked there in my mind many times, but I have never put pencil to paper. To draw it would be to decide what it is. I am not ready. The blank space is not a lack. It is a promise.

This may sound like procrastination. Perhaps it is. But there is a difference between abandoning a thing and tending to it. I tend to my map the way a gardener tends to a plot that is not yet planted. I pull weeds. I turn the soil. I do not know what will grow there, but the tending is the point. The point is not the harvest.

I have a friend who is a novelist. She has been writing the same novel for nine years. It is not finished. She has written six hundred pages, then deleted four hundred. She has changed the protagonist's name from Eleanor to Maren to June. She has moved the setting from a coastal town in Maine to an inland city in Nebraska. She has written the ending seven times and thrown it away seven times. People ask her when the novel will be done. She smiles and says, "It is doing itself." I understand exactly what she means. The novel is not a product. It is a process. The process is the art. The finished book, if it ever comes, will be a snapshot of the process at one moment. But the process will continue, even after the book is published. She will keep writing it in her head. The book is just the part she happened to write down.

This is a dangerous thing to say in a world that demands outcomes. We want deliverables. We want completed checklists. We want the satisfaction of a line drawn through a task. But there is another kind of satisfaction, a slower kind, that comes from staying with something long enough that it becomes a companion. My map is a companion. It asks nothing of me except that I keep it near. It does not care if it is ever finished. In fact, it might prefer not to be. A finished map would be a dead map. It would be a thing I could roll up and put in a drawer and forget. But an unfinished map stays on my desk, waiting. It is a question that never gets old.

I think of the great unfinished works: Schubert's Eighth Symphony, Kafka's novels, the Sagrada Família. The Sagrada Família has been under construction for over a century and is still not finished. But people flock to it because it is unfinished. They want to see the cranes and the scaffolding. They want to see the stone being cut in real time. A finished cathedral is a monument. An unfinished cathedral is a miracle. It is proof that someone is still dreaming.

Maybe that is what I am trying to say. Unfinished things are proof that someone is still dreaming. They are evidence that the world is not yet fixed, that possibilities remain open, that time has not run out. A blank page is terrifying, but it is also full. An unfinished map is not a failure. It is a love letter to the future, written in pencil, never sent.

I do not know if I will ever finish my map. I hope I do not. I hope I die with it still on my desk, the northwest quadrant still blank, the river still uncoiling. I hope someone finds it and wonders what city it was meant to be. Maybe they will add their own streets. Maybe they will erase mine. The map will go on, unfinished, because it is not a thing. It is a place. And places, like people, are never finished.

That is perhaps the deepest truth. We are all unfinished maps. We have blank spaces we are not ready to draw. We have streets that lead nowhere and rivers that double back. We have names for places that no longer exist and places that exist but have no names. And we are always changing, erasing, redrawing. We are not finished. We are not failures. We are alive.

So I will keep my map. I will keep it in pencil, not pen. I will keep the eraser close. I will leave the northwest quadrant blank for as long as it needs to be blank. And when I am gone, I hope the map remains, still unfinished, still becoming, still open to whatever the next hand will bring.
